---
title: "5 · Designs & Clifford Ensembles"
---

Haar randomness is a beautiful benchmark and a practical impossibility. Writing
down a Haar-random unitary on $N$ qubits costs exponentially many parameters. The
fix is to match the Haar measure only where it matters, on its **low moments**.

A **unitary $t$-design** is a finite ensemble whose averages agree with the Haar
average up to the $t$-th moment. Everything in Chapters 3 and 6 depends only on
the second (sometimes fourth) moment, so a 2- or 3-design is "random enough." The
**Clifford group** is the workhorse. It is an exact 3-design, efficiently
sampleable, and classically simulable, yet that very simulability tells us it is
*missing something*.

That missing ingredient is **nonstabilizerness**, or "magic." This part makes
the gap concrete. Clifford circuits can produce near-maximal entanglement, yet
their out-of-time-ordered correlator only ever takes the values $0$ or $4$, 
there is no smooth Lyapunov growth. The **stabilizer Rényi entropy** quantifies
exactly how far a state sits from the stabilizer world, and it is zero precisely
for the states Cliffords can reach.

## Notebooks in this part

- [Clifford OTOCs](../notebooks/ch5/solution_ch5_clifford_otoc.ipynb), why Clifford circuits scramble but have no Lyapunov exponent (the OTOC is $0$ or $4$).
- [Stabilizer Rényi entropy](../notebooks/ch5/solution_ch5_stabilizer_renyi_entropy.ipynb), measuring "magic," the resource beyond entanglement.
